catalog_quote: Stress is generally on the second syllable. Secondary stresses on even-numbered syllables (Echeverria & Contreras 1965:134)

audit.recode_to: weight-sensitive, right-edge (non-strict): main stress on the final syllable if closed, otherwise the penult (right-aligned moraic trochee), CVCV disyllables variable; secondary/stem stress in a left-edge two-syllable window attracted by closed syllables. Sources: Zuniga 2006:63-64 (held), Sadowsky et al. 2013:94, Molineaux 2014:220, Molineaux 2018. Drop 'fixed-strict 01 010 0101...' (E&C 1965 via StressTyp2), keeping E&C as a noted minority description.
audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: (1) The record carries no quotation of its own; its deciding text is StressTyp2 passage 1398, which I confirmed verbatim in the held StressTyp2.sqlite. E&C 1965 itself is not held, but its p.134 rule is quoted verbatim in de Lacy 2014 and Molineaux 2014 (fetched sources now), and E&C's own special rule (b) already allows either syllable in CVCV disyllables, so 'strict 01' overstates even E&C. (2) The coding rests on a database paraphrase of a 1965 four-page phonemic sketch. sources.quote: 'researchers' appetite for clear-cut cases of rhythmic behaviour has led to hurried generalisations about the word-prosodic system of Mapudungun, seeing it as a perfect grid of unstressed and stressed syllables (an iterative, left-right, quantity-insensitive iamb). As de Lacy (2014) has already shown, accounts of this language are ...' [problematic]; the chapter re-derives right-edge weight-sensitive word stress plus morphologically conditioned stem stress.

sources.quote: 'Stress in Mapudungun is non-contrastive. In general, closed syllables tend to attract stress. Words ending in a consonant are stressed on the final syllable ([mɜˈkʊɲ] 'cape, poncho'). Disyllabic words ending in a vowel tend to be stressed on the final syllable in northern and north-central dialects ... and on the penultimate syllable in southern and south-central dialects ... In trisyllabic words, stress tends to fall on the penult if the word ends with an open syllable ([mɜˈwɪθɜ] 'hill'), and on the final syllable otherwise ([mɜt͡ʃɪˈtʊn]). sources.quote: Same informants/recordings as E&C 1965, opposite conclusion: '1) una gran tendencia a la alternancia acentual, y 2) muchas palabras cambian de acento segun su ubicacion ... El acento no es predecible fonemicamente, pero si podria serlo en un plano morfemico ... Es posible tambien que ciertos morfemas tengan acento fijo, por ejemplo: /rume'/ 'bastante', /inche'/ 'yo', /wule'/ 'manana''.

sources.note: The standard English-language reference grammar (Glottolog's top modern grammar, 587 pp) and the only modern description that partly sides with second-syllable main stress (trisyllables kuñífal; 'every second and every last vowel' in long words) while also stating 'stress tends to fall on the vowel before the last consonant'; needed verbatim to state the dissent fairly when recoding. Currently known to us only via Molineaux 2014:59-61 and de Lacy 2014:28.
